Write the introduction to a guide for a REST API that manages calendar bookings. Around 200 words.

# Introduction

The Calendar Bookings API lets you build scheduling applications with straightforward HTTP endpoints.

This guide covers all operations needed to integrate calendar functionality into your application. Whether you're building a personal scheduling tool, a room reservation system, or a service that coordinates team availability, the API provides core primitives: creating bookings, querying time slots, managing cancellations, and checking availability. The API uses standard REST conventions with JSON for all requests and responses. Authentication relies on API keys passed in request headers.

Errors return standard HTTP status codes with structured error details so your client can handle failures gracefully.

Before you start, you'll need an API key. Generate one through your account dashboard or contact support. Once authenticated, you can begin creating events immediately. The guide is organized by task. Each endpoint includes a description of what it does, the required parameters, and examples of typical requests and responses. Common workflows—like checking if a time slot is available before booking it—appear in a recipes section.

We've included curl examples you can run right away and code snippets in Python and JavaScript.

All requests require an API key, which works like a password that identifies you to the API. Generate a key from your account dashboard under API settings. Each request sends this key in the Authorization header at the top of your message, formatted as `Bearer your-api-key-here`. Think of the Authorization header as a container where you tell the API who you are. Treat your key like a password—don't share it or paste it into public sites. If someone gets your key, generate a new one right away and delete the old one. When you send a request without a key or with an incorrect key, the API responds with a 401 Unauthorized error, meaning it rejected your credentials.

All requests require an API key, which works like a password that identifies you to the API. Generate a key from your account dashboard under API settings. Each request sends this key in the Authorization header at the top of your message, formatted as `Bearer your-api-key-here`. Think of the Authorization header as a container where you tell the API who you are. Treat your key like a password—don't share it or paste it into public sites. If someone gets your key, generate a new one right away and delete the old one. When you send a request without a key or with an incorrect key, the API responds with a 401 Unauthorized error, meaning it rejected your credentials.

The API enforces rate limits to prevent abuse. Each API key can make up to 1,000 requests per hour. When you hit this limit, the API returns a 429 Too Many Requests response. Wait a few minutes before sending more requests, or contact support if you need a higher limit for your application.
